title: Telephony and carriers
blurb: A leg and B leg, PSTN versus VoIP, softphones, allowlists, and TLS without invented SIP headers.

lessons.title: A leg and B leg meet on a media server
lessons.summary: The contact-to-CXone side is the A leg. The CXone-to-agent side is the B leg. Inbound treats A as ingress and B as egress. A transfer adds a second B leg.
objectives: Name both legs
Classify ingress and egress
Add the second B leg for a transfer

p: The contact calls a local or toll-free number. The call crosses the PSTN and enters CXone. That portion is the A leg, inbound or ingress. CXone queues it for agents with the right skills.
The agent is logged into MAX, Agent Workspace, or Salesforce Agent over the internet. The portion between CXone and the agent is the B leg, outbound or egress. The legs connect on a media server.
A transfer places a second B leg to the next agent. All three legs meet on the media server, then the first agent drops.
On an outbound call, both legs originate in CXone and are egress. CXone can dial for the agent when that is configured.

choices: In the browser only, with no server

quiz.why: Then the first agent can drop.

lab.title: Draw inbound and outbound
steps: Inbound: A ingress, B egress.

Name the media server.

lessons.title: PSTN is DID or TFN. VoIP stays on the agent leg.
lessons.summary: CXone classifies DID or toll-free traffic as PSTN. It supports PSTN on the A leg and restricts VoIP to the agent leg, unless a UCaaS partner arrangement says otherwise.
objectives: Define PSTN as the page does
Keep VoIP on the B leg
Send A-leg VoIP to the account representative

p: PSTN is the traditional phone system. CXone classifies phone traffic routed by DID or toll-free number as PSTN. VoIP carries calls over the internet and needs a VoIP phone or a softphone.
Both can be used on the agent leg. CXone supports PSTN on the A leg and restricts VoIP to the agent leg.
Some UCaaS partners allow VoIP on the A leg. If you need that, talk to the account representative. This lesson does not list partners.
Call Quality Explorer is the report named for latency, jitter, or dropped calls.

lessons.title: Integrated Softphone is not the word WebRTC
lessons.summary: Integrated Softphone is built in, with nothing to install. Softphone is a separate install. WebRTC is the Chrome technology Integrated Softphone uses. The names are not synonyms.
objectives: Separate the two products
Use WebRTC only as the technology
Say an allowlist is required

p: If the agent leg is VoIP, CXone offers Integrated Softphone, built into the platform so there is nothing to install, and Softphone, a separate application that must be installed.

The page says Integrated Softphone is sometimes called WebRTC, and that the two names do not refer to the same thing. WebRTC is the communications technology in the Chrome browser. It is what Integrated Softphone uses.
If you use Integrated Softphone, IP addresses must be added to your allowlist. The connectivity page does not paste that list. Do not copy a list from an old screenshot into this lab.
A browser matrix beyond the Chrome mention is not on this page. Treat other browsers as uncertain until you open a current matrix.

lessons.title: Numbers, RespOrg, and the voice PoP
lessons.summary: The preferred toll-free path is to make CXone the RespOrg. Local numbers can be ported. Other arrivals are remote call forwarding, an independent carrier, or your PBX. A voice PoP is the carrier's PSTN gateway.
objectives: Prefer RespOrg for toll-free
List the other three arrivals
Define PoP and SIP trunk as the page does

p: The preferred option is to authorize CXone as the Responsible Organization for the toll-free numbers you want to use. Local numbers can be ported if you want that.

Other methods: remote call forwarding, directly from an independent carrier, or directly from your PBX. If CXone is the RespOrg, you order more numbers through CXone. Otherwise you order them from your carrier.
A voice Point of Presence is the physical place your carrier connects to the PSTN. It is the gateway for calls to and from the carrier.

A SIP trunk is a virtual connection from your PBX to the carrier. It can use a traditional phone line, VoIP, or a dedicated connection such as MPLS. RFC 3261 is the SIP protocol. It is not a list of CXone headers.

steps.label: DNIS
steps.detail: Professional Services configures phone DNIS before the point of contact.

steps.label: SIP
steps.detail: Protocol is RFC 3261. Headers are not invented here.

quiz.q: RFC 3261 tells you CXone's proprietary headers.
choices: No. It is the SIP protocol.
quiz.why: Cite it for SIP, not for a header cookbook.

lessons.title: Allowlists, proxies, and TLS 1.2
lessons.summary: Firewalls need the current domains, addresses, and ports. CXone does not support traffic-inspection proxies. Connections require at least TLS 1.2 and one of the ciphers the page lists for that direction.
objectives: Refuse a stale IP list
Decline inspection proxies
Quote TLS 1.2 and the cipher direction

p: The firewall section says domains, IP addresses, and ports must be allowed. The approved set is an allowlist. Copy it from the current help, not from this lesson.

CXone does not support traffic-inspection proxies. The reasons named are latency, the proxy's own maintenance, routing-policy mistakes, and third-party troubleshooting. If you use a proxy anyway, you configure it yourself.

CXone requires at least TLS 1.2. Inbound, from CXone to your servers, the page lists 0x009E, 0xC013, 0xC02B, and 0xC02C, and recommends supporting more than one. Outbound, from your servers to CXone, it lists 0xC02F and 0xC030, and recommends both.
Those codes are the page's list. A design that needs a different cipher has to take that up outside this lab.

steps.label: Outbound
steps.detail: Two codes. Support both if you can.

quiz.why: The live page owns the list.

lessons.title: Your tenant sits on a named cluster
lessons.summary: CXone runs in AWS data centers that NiCE does not own. NiCE manages the software. A cluster has a letter-and-number name. You need your cluster when you work on connectivity.
objectives: Separate AWS ownership from NiCE software
Know you have a cluster name
Not treat the examples as your cluster

p: Users reach CXone with a browser and an internet connection. There is no on-site computer running the CXone platform itself. The computers are in data centers owned and operated by other organizations. The page says NiCE uses Amazon Web Services. AWS owns the hardware. NiCE manages the software.
Servers are grouped into a cluster. Examples on the page are C14, E39, and M33. Those are examples, not your name.
The page says that when you work on connectivity you need to know which cluster you run on. Allowlists and paths are how you reach that cluster.
A Teams recording bot deployed in a NiCE Azure account, on the Multi-ACD page, is a different sentence. Do not collapse Azure and AWS.

lessons.title: The carrier, the PoP, and CXone are three owners
lessons.summary: The carrier brings the internet and the voice PoP. CXone starts when the number, email, or chat is a point of contact. SIP header recipes and OPTIONS timers are not in the connectivity page.
objectives: Give the carrier the PoP
Give CXone the point of contact
Stop before invented SIP details

p: The carrier is the company that provides the internet connection. The voice PoP is that carrier's PSTN gateway. A SIP trunk connects your PBX to the carrier.
Once a phone number, email address, or chat window is a point of contact, CXone handles the interaction and routes it to agents. That handoff is the connectivity page's story.
Every organization's requirements are unique. The page tells you to work with the account representative. It does not list CXone-specific SIP headers, codecs, or OPTIONS timers.
RFC 3261 remains the protocol citation. A header not on a CXone page is not a CXone requirement.

choices: The number, email, or chat is a point of contact
